01 Antidepressants · class card

SSRIs

selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors · citalopram · escitalopram · fluoxetine · fluvoxamine · paroxetine · sertraline

Key point
  • Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) block serotonin reuptake early nausea, headache, insomnia and anxiety; later sexual dysfunction and weight gain
  • Class risks: suicidal thoughts under 25 (boxed warning), hyponatremia, and bleeding with an anti-inflammatory or an anticoagulant
  • Citalopram: dose-dependent QT prolongation, avoided after a recent heart attack; paroxetine: the most interactions and a first-trimester heart-defect signal; fluoxetine: long half-life, so no taper
Drugs

Citalopram Celexa: dose-dependent QT prolongation, fewest interactions

Escitalopram Lexapro: few interactions

Fluoxetine Prozac: long half-life, so no taper is needed; strong cytochrome P450 2D6 (CYP2D6) inhibitor

Fluvoxamine: strong cytochrome P450 1A2 (CYP1A2) inhibitor

Paroxetine Paxil: most interactions, most discontinuation symptoms, anticholinergic

Sertraline Zoloft: few interactions

Mechanism

Serotonin transporter blocked more serotonin in the synapse longer postsynaptic stimulation Serotonin receptorsType 1 receptors carry the antidepressant and anti-anxiety effect; type 2 receptors bring anxiety, insomnia and sexual dysfunction; type 3 receptors bring nausea and headache. Dopamine and norepinephrine are barely touched.

Few anticholinergic or cardiac conduction effects wide safety margin; isolated overdose is usually well tolerated

Uses

Depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder, panic, generalized and social anxiety, premenstrual dysphoric disorder; fluoxetine for bulimia nervosa Other usesSSRIs also treat premature ejaculation and menopausal hot flashes (paroxetine, citalopram).

Adverse effects

Early: nausea, headache, insomnia or sleepiness, anxiety, dizziness Sertraline labelThe Zoloft label also lists diarrhea, tremor, indigestion, less appetite and sweating among the most common effects.

Later: sexual dysfunction in up to half, weight gain In practiceHigher in the Merck Manual: sexual dysfunction above half of patients, most often trouble reaching orgasm.

Hyponatremia, often from the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH), higher risk over 65 Drug causes of SIADH"Can't Concentrate Serum Na+": carbamazepine, cyclophosphamide, SSRIs and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) can all cause SIADH.

Paroxetine: anticholinergic; fluoxetine: agitation, early appetite loss

Abrupt stop of a short half-life SSRI such as paroxetine: flu-like, neurologic and psychiatric symptoms within days

Monitoring

Before starting: screen for bipolar disorder

Older adults: serum sodium

QT prolongation on citalopramDose-dependent; label maximum 40 mg a day, 20 mg over age 60 or with hepatic impairment Citalopram labelThe Celexa label also avoids it with congenital long QT, a slow heart rate, low potassium or magnesium, uncompensated heart failure or another QT-prolonging drug, and checks electrolytes when they may run low.

If a patient with a recent heart attack needs an SSRI, choose sertraline or escitalopram, not citalopram.

A citalopram overdose can still bring torsade de pointes, and it may be delayed: keep the heart monitored

Suicidal thoughts under 25Boxed warning: more suicidal thoughts in children and adults under 25 in short-term studies

If a patient of any age starts an antidepressant, choose a close watch for worsening mood and suicidal thinking.

Paroxetine in pregnancyFirst-trimester exposure: under a 2-fold rise in cardiac malformations

If an SSRI is needed in pregnancy, choose sertraline or escitalopram over paroxetine.

Newborn riskAny SSRI late in pregnancy, paroxetine included, can cause persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn. On the Zoloft label, newborns exposed to an SSRI late in the third trimester have needed prolonged hospital care, breathing support and tube feeding.

Interactions, by result
Combined withResultRule
A monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI), or one stopped inside its washout Serotonin syndrome, potentially life-threateningNever together
Tramadol, linezolid, a triptan, dextromethorphan, ondansetron or St John's wortSerotonin syndrome Watch for clonus and hyperreflexia; avoid St John's wort
Aspirin, a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID), warfarin or another anticoagulantBleeding risk can rise, including GI Platelet serotoninOn an SSRI, platelets take up less serotonin, and they rely on it to stop bleeding.Counsel on bleeding; check the international normalized ratio (INR) on warfarin
Tamoxifen, with paroxetine or fluoxetineLess active tamoxifen metabolite (CYP2D6)Choose one with little CYP2D6 inhibition
Tricyclic antidepressants or metoprolol, with paroxetine or fluoxetineTheir levels can rise (CYP2D6)Lower their dose if needed
Tizanidine, ramelteon, theophylline or clozapine, with fluvoxamineTheir levels may rise (CYP1A2)Never tizanidine or ramelteon; theophylline to a third of its dose, with levels

How NBME framed it

Setup Sertraline stopped last month; a day of headache, aches, diarrhea, anxiety, fine tremor

Offered alcohol use disorder, influenza, migraine, pregnancy, an anxiety disorder

Deciding clue: the typical flu-like and hyperarousal picture after an SSRI stop

Answer SSRI withdrawal (discontinuation syndrome)

Setup Paroxetine stopped abruptly 2 weeks ago; dizziness worse on turning the head, paresthesias

Offered benign positional vertigo, multiple sclerosis, SIADH, functional neurologic disorder, illness anxiety disorder (hypochondriasis)

Deciding clue: a short half-life drug stopped abruptly

Answer SSRI withdrawal (discontinuation syndrome)

Practice
  1. 61-year-old man, 3 weeks after an anterior myocardial infarction low mood, anhedonia and poor sleep for a month; wants a medicine takes aspirin, metoprolol and a statin electrocardiogram: sinus rhythm, corrected QT at the upper limit of normal → Citalopram → its dose-dependent QT prolongation makes it the SSRI to avoid after a recent myocardial infarction; sertraline and escitalopram are the first choices, with few drug interactions
  2. 46-year-old woman takes tamoxifen after surgery for estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer two months of low mood, poor sleep and guilt meets criteria for major depressive disorder; an SSRI is planned no other medicines → Paroxetine → a strong inhibitor of cytochrome P450 2D6, it lowers the active metabolite of tamoxifen; citalopram inhibits that enzyme only weakly, and escitalopram has few drug interactions
  3. 34-year-old woman started sertraline for major depressive disorder 2 weeks ago on a full dose since; sleep a little better, mood unchanged mild nausea in the first days, now gone no suicidal thoughts → Continue sertraline at the same dose → response usually starts at 2 to 3 weeks and can take up to 8; an SSRI gets 6 weeks at full dose before any change, and an abrupt stop can bring discontinuation symptoms
